content: 1. The analysis used a threshold of 10 per 1000 patients to determine the presence of an important effect. The 95% confidence interval (CI) crossed this threshold, indicating the possibility of both significant benefit and harm. 2. The review did not provide baseline risk or forest plots. Baseline risk was inferred from the control arms of other antihypertensive trials. 3. The results were derived from a network meta-analysis that included five trials: two directly comparing angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) to placebo, two comparing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis) to placebo, and one comparing ACEis to ARBs. 4. When assessing the certainty of no important effect using the 10 per 1000 threshold, the upper limit of the 95% CI crossed this threshold, suggesting the potential for significant harm. 5. Another network meta-analysis included five trials: one comparing ARBs to placebo, three comparing ACEis to placebo, and one comparing ACEis to ARBs. 6. The point estimates showed significant variability in both direction and magnitude of effect, with some confidence intervals not overlapping. High statistical heterogeneity was observed, as indicated by an I-squared value of 64%. 7. The authors did not provide detailed risk of bias assessments. However, some included studies were judged to have low Jadad scores. 8. Cognitive impairment/dementia, myocardial infarction, heart failure, end-stage kidney disease, and blood pressure reduction outcomes were not reported. 9. The included studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in domains such as incomplete outcome data and unclear risk of bias in other domains. 10. For non-selective beta-blockers, the 95% CI for stroke outcomes was reported. 11. The point estimates varied significantly in direction and magnitude of effect, with some confidence intervals not overlapping. High statistical heterogeneity was observed, with an I-squared value of 68%. 12. The confidence interval crossed the line of no effect, suggesting that the difference could be significantly less or more. The extremes of the confidence interval could lead to different clinical decisions. 13. The two trials contributing most of the weight to the pooled estimate (>90%) were judged to have unclear risk of bias in the domain of incomplete outcome data. 14. The certainty of no important effect was rated using a threshold of 10 per 1000 patients. The upper limit of the 95% CI crossed this threshold, suggesting potential harm. 15. The two trials contributing most of the weight to the pooled estimate (>80%) were judged to have high risk of bias in the domains of blinding of participants and personnel, and unclear risk of bias in allocation concealment and incomplete outcome data. 16. The two trials contributing most of the weight to the pooled estimate (>75%) were judged to have high risk of bias in the domain of allocation concealment. 20. One of the two included studies was judged to have high risk of bias in the domain of allocation concealment. 21. The certainty of no important effect was rated using a threshold of 10 per 1000 patients. The lower and upper ends of the 95% CI crossed this threshold, suggesting potential benefit and harm. 22. The trial contributing most of the weight to the pooled estimate (99%) was judged to have unclear risk in the domain of blinding of outcome assessment. 23. The extremes of the confidence interval suggest the possibility of a small benefit and a small harm, leading to different clinical decisions. 24. Seven out of the ten included studies were observational. 25. Two of the included studies were open-label extensions of trials, contributing only 16% of the weight to the pooled estimates. The review stated that all included studies were of high quality based on the Newcastle-Ottawa scale, but no further details were provided. 26.
